Herald letters
An interesting letter whether you are religious or not!
THE question is not whether “climate science” and the deification of “carbon neutrality” is a cult, but rather whether or not it is a false religion?
Last Sunday morning, I listened to a sermon based on the confrontation which took place on Mount Carmel between Elijah and the false prophets of Baal. It wasn’t the first sermon that I had heard on that subject. However, it was only after reading a letter in The Herald that it struck me that something significant had never been mentioned about this encounter that may be highly relevant for such a time as this.
The letter entitled “Climate science is no cult, despite what many critics continue to claim” (The Herald on Ssunday, November 15) was making the counterclaim that climate science wasn’t a cult.
However, the close juxtaposition of my reading this letter with the Biblical
account in 1 Kings 18:16-46 highlighted something very important that I had not seen highlighted previously.
The important point is this: the authentication that Elijah was a true prophet of the only true God came in verse 38 when “the fire of the Lord fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice”.
God had miraculously intervened and it is noteworthy that this divine intervention took the form of an act of combustion. It wasn’t carbon neutral.
The sacrifice offered by the false prophets of the false god Baal remained unburned and essentially carbon neutral relative to that of Elijah.
Perhaps one modern application of this text might be that our nation should spend more time seeking to worship the one true God rather than the god of carbon neutrality.
We need to turn away from this worship of “environmentalism” per se to worshipful responsible stewardship of the planet and natural resources God has given us for the benefit of mankind. Dr Steven William Welsh, Western Isles.

records.bodyText:
BLADE delivery schedules for Sanquhar II Wind Farm for next week have been confirmed from the firm in charge.
Delays have been reported through the transfer route as components make their way to the wind farm.
The deliveries form part of the construction of the 44-turbine Sanquhar II Wind Farm, a major renewable energy development spanning parts of East Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway.
According to the latest delivery timetable released by CWP Energy, turbine blades will be transported from King George V Docks in Glasgow to the project's transfer area this coming Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
The developer states that deliveries will depart King George V Docks from 9pm onwards each evening.
No deliveries are currently planned for Friday, November 27, Saturday, November 28 or Sunday, November 29.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Wind farms in Scotland were paid an eyewatering £470 million in constraint payments in October 2026. 
There are 2.57 million households in Scotland - thats £182 per Scottish household paid in constraint payments in October alone.  Of course Scottish households do not pick up the bill for all constraints - they are added to everyone’s electricity bills across the UK. 
The total bill for constraint payments across the UK was £744 million for October.. 
And we wonder why electricity bills are so high??
The National Energy System Operator recognises too many wind farms are planned in Scotland and that even the proposed grid upgrades would not remove the need for constraint payments. 
Most of the £470,000,000 will go to the (ultimately overseas based) shareholders and owners…..

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText: 𝐃𝐲𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝How much additional electricity infrastructure do we actually need, and are we making the best possible use of what we already have?The question of the need for new electricity infrastructure is one that deserves rather more scrutiny than it receives, from the Government/s and NGOs at least - campaign groups/Ian Kelly, the planning consultant/barristers acting for groups - all have asked the question, time after time.We regularly hear about the requirement for additional transmission lines, substations and network reinforcement, but there is another side to the equation: how much more could we achieve by making better use of existing infrastructure?One technology that illustrates this particularly well is Dynamic Line Rating (DLR). We said in our summary of the Public Accounts Committee meeting that we would return to this subject. Firstly, a word about what  Dynamic Line Rating is.Traditionally, overhead transmission lines have operated within predetermined capacity limits, based on conservative assumptions about the conditions in which the conductors are operating.However, the amount of electricity an overhead line can safely carry is affected by environmental conditions. Wind speed, ambient temperature and solar radiation all influence the temperature of the conductor and its ability to dissipate heat.DLR uses sensors and monitoring technology to assess these conditions and calculate how much electricity a conductor can safely carry at a given time.For example, where wind conditions provide greater cooling, a line may be able to carry more electricity than its conventional rating would permit. Conversely, under hotter or less favourable conditions, its available capacity may be lower.The advantage is that the network operator can make use of capacity that would otherwise remain unavailable under a fixed rating.It doesn't eliminate the need for new infrastructure where additional enduring capacity is required, but it can improve utilisation of existing lines, increase available transmission capacity and potentially reduce the need for, or urgency of, some reinforcement.𝐃𝐲𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧During the Kintore–Tealing Public Local Inquiry, Brian Wade, who submitted evidence on technological alternatives, raised a wider question about the use of existing transmission infrastructure.In his written submission, Brian identified several technologies falling under the general heading of Grid Enhancing Technologies. These include Dynamic Line Rating, reconductoring using modern high-capacity conductors, Flexible AC Transmission Systems and topology control.The technologies work in different ways, but share an important objective: increasing the capacity or improving the utilisation of the existing electricity network.Reconductoring, for example, can involve replacing conventional conductors with modern, higher-capacity alternatives, potentially allowing significantly greater power flows without constructing an entirely new transmission route. The extent of any increase depends on the capabilities and limitations of the existing infrastructure.Brian also raised the question of whether alternatives such as underground HVDC connections and greater integration of offshore transmission networks had been adequately considered in the TKUP proposals.His wider argument was that infrastructure options should be assessed not simply on their initial construction costs, but on their whole-life costs, technical performance and environmental and community impacts.These are questions which deserve consideration whenever major new transmission infrastructure is proposed. DLR is one example of how technology can make better use of existing assets, but it is not the only one. 𝐒𝐒𝐄𝐍'𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐮𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐲An article in the John O'Groat Journal on 25 September 2026 which we covered on 5 October, reported that SSEN Transmission had installed DLR technology on more than 300km of overhead transmission lines between Beauly and Dounreay.The article reported that the system had gone live on the first DLR-enabled circuit in the north of Scotland.SSEN Transmission also reported that DLR technology installed elsewhere on its network had delivered nearly £300 million in savings for consumers since 2021.The article highlighted the potential for DLR to reduce constraint costs by allowing more electricity to flow through existing infrastructure when conditions permit.This is particularly relevant in Scotland, where renewable generation is frequently constrained because the transmission network cannot always accommodate the electricity available to it.Making better use of existing transmission capacity is therefore an important part of addressing the problem.𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐞 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬?The subject of constraint costs also arose during the Public Accounts Committee's examination of the electricity system.The Committee Chair returned to the projected £7–8 billion figure, questioning why there had been no updated assessment since the original analysis in 2024.Fintan Slye explained that the next analysis was due in the following months. Jonathan Brearley acknowledged that he was not happy with the figure and that work was under way to bring it down.The Chair also questioned why the costs and implications of individual grid upgrades were not being made available, including the cost of not undertaking them. The discussion highlighted the importance of bringing together the timing and cost of network upgrades with the generation expected to come online, in order to understand their combined effect on constraint costs.When the Chair returned to the £7–8 billion estimate, Slye identified a number of shorter-term measures being introduced to reduce costs, including the rollout of Dynamic Line Rating in conjunction with transmission companies.He explained that the technology was being installed on transmission lines to maximise the amount of power that could be transmitted, according to the prevailing conditions and the sag of the conductor.This exchange is worth noting for two reasons. Firstly, it demonstrates that the projected constraint-cost figure was not static and that updated analysis was needed. Secondly, it confirms that technological and operational improvements, including DLR, were already being deployed as part of the effort to reduce costs.It also raises a wider question: when decisions are being made about the need for new electricity infrastructure, how fully are the potential benefits of making better use of existing infrastructure being taken into account?The relevant exchanges are in images.𝐌𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞, 𝐒𝐒𝐄𝐍 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧 £𝟖.𝟕 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐎𝐟𝐠𝐞𝐦Yesterday, SSEN Distribution announced that it had submitted its business plan to Ofgem for the next electricity distribution price-control period, ED3, covering 2028–2033.The proposed investment is £8.7 billion.Of this, £1.3 billion has already been approved by Ofgem, with SSEN seeking approval for the remaining £7.4 billion.There is also the possibility of a further £1.5 billion through in-period uncertainty mechanisms, which could take total expenditure to £10.2 billion.The plan, titled 'Electrified. Resilient. Affordable', covers SSEN's two distribution licence areas: the north of Scotland and central southern England.It is intended to accommodate forecast growth in electricity demand, support electrification of transport and heating, facilitate new connections and improve network resilience.Among its principal proposals are:- Increasing network capacity by 24%.- Deploying 13.4GW of flexibility, six times the level in the current ED2 period.- Maintaining overall network reliability of 99.98%.- Rebuilding or undergrounding approximately 350km of high-risk overhead lines.- Replacing around 250km of climate-vulnerable cabling.- Offering 5GW of early-access connections.SSEN is also proposing to keep the distribution element of household bills flat in real terms until 2030, subject to the necessary regulatory and government approvals.It is important to understand that this is a distribution investment plan. It is not an SSEN Transmission investment programme. The two businesses operate at different levels of the electricity network.𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐥𝐞𝐱: 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞There is something particularly interesting in the ED3 business plan.SSEN recognises that simply building additional infrastructure is not necessarily the most efficient way of meeting future demand.Its proposed Build and Flex approach is intended to make greater use of existing network capacity, using flexibility where possible and reinforcing the network where additional enduring capacity is required.The plan identifies six ways in which flexibility can be used, including:- Replacing conventional reinforcement where flexibility is economically viable.- Managing uncertainty in the timing and scale of future demand.- Bridging the gap where justified reinforcement cannot be delivered immediately.- Providing temporary capacity to accelerate customer connections.- Managing planned and unplanned outages.- Coordinating the use of the network through operational signals and flexible assets.SSEN estimates that its enhanced Build and Flex approach could defer £195 million of capital expenditure during ED3.It is also proposing an agile funding mechanism which would allow it to proceed with construction if the anticipated flexibility does not materialise or if new requirements emerge.In other words, SSEN acknowledges that better utilisation of existing network capacity can reduce the amount of new infrastructure required, or at least defer investment until the need becomes clearer.𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐥𝐬𝐨 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝The ED3 plan includes a separate investment programme of £107 million in smarter network capabilities.One of its proposals is to introduce dynamic voltage management across 50% of network load. SSEN estimates that this could release more than 1GW of additional capacity for low-carbon technologies, including electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps, without major reinforcement.This is not the same technology as Dynamic Line Rating. DLR assesses the thermal capacity of overhead conductors, whereas dynamic voltage management concerns the control of voltage on distribution networks.Nevertheless, both illustrate the wider principle of making better use of existing infrastructure through improved monitoring, control and operational management.𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝?We are not suggesting that all additional infrastructure can be avoided -  electricity demand is changing, electrification is increasing, and there will undoubtedly be parts of the network where reinforcement is necessary.However, there is a distinction between establishing that additional capacity will be needed and determining how best to provide it.SSEN's own ED3 business plan recognises this. It says that it assesses different demand scenarios, considers flexibility alongside conventional reinforcement and uses sensitivity testing to identify investment that is genuinely required within the price-control period.It also acknowledges that flexibility can avoid unnecessary reinforcement and that investment decisions should adapt as the evidence develops.The question is whether the same degree of scrutiny is consistently applied across the wider electricity network.SSEN Distribution's £8.7 billion plan covers both northern Scotland and central southern England. Its Scottish distribution network serves around 800,000 customers, but accounts for nearly 39% of the combined network length. The southern English operation has a different demand profile, including significant concentrations of new demand.The entire investment programme does not relate only to Scotland, and the circumstances in the two licence areas are not interchangeable.  We will be returning to this subject in another post.But the wider point remains.As we see proposals for major new transmission infrastructure, including the overhead lines and substations required to accommodate projected increases in electricity flows, we should be asking:- Have the capabilities of existing infrastructure been fully assessed?- Have technologies such as Dynamic Line Rating been properly considered?- Have flexibility and other operational solutions been evaluated alongside conventional reinforcement?- Are demand forecasts sufficiently robust, and have alternative scenarios been tested?- Is the proposed infrastructure necessary now, or could some investment be deferred while existing capacity is used more effectively?The answer will not always be that new infrastructure can be avoided. But it should be possible to demonstrate why it is necessary, and why the alternatives are insufficient.𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭. records.title: NO to East Havering Data Centre in Upminster (Residents Group)

source.name: NO to East Havering Data Centre in Upminster (Residents Group)
source.label: Facebook · NO to East Havering Data Centre in Upminster (Residents Group)

records.bodyText:
Interesting that Havering included the update on water reservoir levels and the continuing water restrictions in their latest newsletter. This is on the the same day as one of the Upminster and Cranham Councillors (HARA) has been commenting on Facebook yesterday about the proposed data centre and saying how the next LDO draft and proposed water usage has changed now. So there’s no need to worry about the water guzzling data centre as apparently it will use much less, she says. You know who, without me naming her. Really? How does she know this, and why does she know this? Why is she still promoting this project for Digital Reef? We would have hoped that if discussions were taking place and changes were being made, resident’s would have been engaged this time. They don’t have to speak with me, I know I’m not their favourite person, but they can engage with any number  of you out there.  
We were always told that ‘Councillors don’t get involved in Planning’ when we used to ask for engagement.  But this one seems to have detailed knowledge of what’s about to be published in the next round of the LDO consultation. 
What do you think about this?
Protect the Greenbelt, transparency ….
